docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text: Documentation for people working on VOGON itself.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. VOGON helps and gets out of the way. It does not impose heavy workflows or bureaucracy.
  2. The process comes from the host project's validation plan, not from VOGON.
  3. A skipped or late step is reported, never blocked.
  4. VOGON never approves or signs. People do.
  5. Evidence never comes from a model.
  6. All work is reviewed by a different agent.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
VOGON is a Claude Code plugin installed into a host project: the repository of a regulated (GxP) software project. It carries out the steps of the GxP process that do not need a person. The plugin is a set of skills, the sub-agents they start, and scripts for the work that must give the same result every time: vogon id allocates record ids, vogon approve records an approval, and vogon trace builds the traceability matrix. All model work is done by Claude Code; the Python code calls no language model (DEC-005). The design follows the principles.

The rules every skill applies are in src/vogon/references/common.md, and each skill's steps, loops, stops and outputs in src/vogon/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md. Vocabulary defines the terms, and Records the record format and the state file.

docs.title: Scope and roles
docs.text:
The host project is written in Python, tested with pytest and kept in git. Skills name each external system by its role, never by product, and reach it only through the system vogon/project/vogon.yaml names for that role, through the MCP connectors of the session.

Role Example system When no system is configured Repository host GitHub The skill tells the person and skips the steps that need it Tracker Jira, GitHub Issues vogon approve records approvals Test manager Xray vogon trace builds the matrix Document system The company's controlled document system Documents are kept in the repository, in vogon/documents/<release>/ Meetings, mail, chat Teams, Outlook, Slack The skill tells the person and skips that source

A tracker holds approvals when tracking.md states an approval transition for the requirement item type. An approval recorded by vogon approve carries the approver's git identity, which the approver does not re-enter at approval, so it is not an electronic signature under 21 CFR Part 11. A tracker or test manager transition is one only when the workflow makes the approver re-enter their credentials at that transition; vogon:init reports each approval transition that does not.

VOGON never decides an approval and never signs (CON-001). A change to a live system is approved in the host project's own change control system, and its requirements, tests and documents go through the same skills (DEC-026).

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
One skill per task a person starts. Each runs in the main Claude Code session.

# Step Skill Produces Approved by 1 Configure vogon:init vogon/project/vogon.yaml, the validation plan in vogon/sources/, the .gitignore and conftest.py lines A person, on the pull request 2 File the sources vogon:requirements Checked summaries of meetings, mail and chat; filed documents with their markdown copies 3 Draft and check the records vogon:requirements Requirements with acceptance criteria and risk fields; facts, constraints and decisions 4 Send the requirements for approval vogon:requirements The pull request with REQ-*.md and REQ-*.json; tracker items where a tracker is configured 5 Approve the requirements vogon:approve, or the tracker An approved entry in REQ-*.json, or the tracker's approval transition where a tracker holds approvals Product Owner 6 Write the test procedures vogon:tests Test procedures, where tests.md requires them The roles tests.md names 7 Choose a requirement vogon:next The ready and blocked lists; the tracker item assigned 8 Plan vogon:implement A checked plan, and a planned entry once approved A developer 9 Write the code, tests and documentation vogon:implement Checked code, tests and documentation, all tests passing, in one pull request A person, on the repository host 10 Release vogon:release The documents documents.md lists, the traceability matrix and the results, filed The roles documents.md names

Different requirements are at different steps at the same time. Step 6 comes before step 7 or after step 9, as tests.md states; a project that needs no test procedures skips it. A change to an approved requirement appends a changed entry and returns the requirement to step 5.

The default checklists are in src/vogon/skills/requirements/references/, src/vogon/skills/tests/references/ and src/vogon/skills/implement/references/. A project replaces one with a file of the same name in vogon/project/checklists/.

docs.title: Start of a skill
docs.text: Tasks happen weeks apart, by different developers, in any order, so a skill does not assume an earlier task ran. Every skill except vogon:init first reads the process files it needs, deriving any that is missing or outdated, then the requirements it concerns, their state files and the sources those link, and reports every difference. When a task was skipped, the skill does what still applies and reports the gap, such as code merged with no plan (common.md "Start of every skill").

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Every skill that produces work runs it in a loop of rounds. The main agent, the session the skill runs in, coordinates and never writes the work. Its context holds the task, file paths and summaries of sub-agent logs, so it stays small over a long task. Sub-agents write and evaluate in their own contexts, each given every input it needs; independent units run in parallel. An evaluator never changes the work. The main agent judges the result and can overrule an evaluator, because it sees every evaluator's findings and the whole task, and each evaluator takes one perspective.

The finding levels, the limit of 5 rounds and the log formats are in common.md "The loop"; each SKILL.md lists its writers and evaluators in its "Loops" table.

docs.title: Stops for a person
docs.text: A skill stops for an approval, a plan review, a finding that needs a choice, a gap in the validation plan, the tracker and test manager names read from example items, a developer's instruction during coding, and a missing input. Nothing else waits for confirmation. common.md "Stops for a person" states who each goes to.

docs.title: Project configuration and process files
docs.text:
vogon/project/vogon.yaml states the system for each role, the holders of each approval role, the modules and the options. vogon:init writes it from src/vogon/templates/vogon.yaml; it is YAML because the scripts read it.

The validation plan is filed in vogon/sources/ as the original and a markdown copy (Sources). It stays the host project's controlled document, and VOGON never edits either copy. The process files in vogon/project/ are VOGON's reading of the plan: tracking.md (tracker and test manager item types, fields, approval transitions), requirements.md (requirement form, risk method, approver and timing), tests.md (test procedures, test environment, how the suite runs), traceability.md, documents.md (the documents VOGON drafts) and release.md.

A skill derives a process file when it first needs it, and again when a newer plan is held. Each statement cites its plan section; the developer answers a gap, and the answer is recorded with their name and date. The procedure is in src/vogon/references/process-files.md, the topics in src/vogon/templates/.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Records are markdown files under vogon/ in the host repository (Records). Each takes its id from vogon id, never from choosing a number. Two branches can take the same id before either pushes, so a skill runs vogon id --check and renumbers before it opens a pull request.

Transcripts, mail and chat contain personal data, and some countries restrict keeping meeting transcripts, so they are downloaded to the gitignored vogon/tmp/ and deleted after use; only a checked summary is committed to vogon/sources/. Attached and shared files are kept as the original and a markdown copy, and a long file is read only in a sub-agent's context. A requirement whose only source is code describes current behaviour, defects included, so the developer confirms it is intended (src/vogon/skills/requirements/SKILL.md, step 8).

docs.title: Approval of requirements
docs.text:
The Product Owner approves requirements; vogon.yaml lists the holders under product_owner. Where no tracker holds approvals, vogon approve records the approval on the Product Owner's explicit instruction. Where a tracker holds approvals, the Product Owner approves with the tracker's transition, and the tracker is the only record of the approval: a skill reads it from the item and nothing copies it into the repository. A skill reports requirement text in the tracker that differs from REQ-*.md, and the developer resolves it as a change to the requirement.

Where no tracker holds approvals, a requirement is approved when REQ-*.json on the default branch has an approved entry after its latest changed entry. Where a tracker holds approvals, it is approved when its item is in the approved state through a transition dated after the latest changed entry. A skill changes an approved requirement only with the developer's agreement, and appends a changed entry, so it needs approval again (common.md "Approval of a requirement").

docs.title: State of a requirement
docs.text: REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>.json records the steps done to the requirement (Records; the entries are defined in src/vogon/references/common.md "State-file entries"). An entry other than approved points at the pull request, commit or tracker item that holds the step. That source is the evidence: a skill checks it before acting on an entry and reports a difference. An approval is decided by the state file on the default branch alone.

docs.title: Risk
docs.text: Each requirement carries gxp_impact and risk, each with its reason, from the moment it is drafted, so a reader can challenge a value. The values and method are in src/vogon/references/records.md, overridden by requirements.md where the validation plan states them; requirements.md also states who approves them and when. Project-level risk documents the plan lists, such as a risk log or a data integrity risk assessment, are separate documents, approved by the roles the plan names.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The pytest code is the test case. Each test names the requirements it verifies in @pytest.mark.req("REQ-PRN-12"), and, where procedures exist, its procedure in @pytest.mark.procedure("<id>"). The link is on the test because whoever changes a test edits its marker in the same edit (DEC-006). Requirement ids are not written in implementation code; commits name them. A test with no marker is allowed and is not evidence. VOGON writes tests from the requirement's intent, never from what the code does. It writes no mocks unless the project authorizes them, because needing a mock indicates a problem in the design.

A test procedure is a document of numbered steps, each with its expected result. tests.md states whether the project needs procedures, whether they are written before development or generated from the tests, and who approves them. vogon:tests imposes no order of its own.

docs.title: Code from requirements
docs.text: vogon:implement has a sub-agent write a plan, vogon/plans/plan_<slug>.md, in the format of src/vogon/skills/implement/references/plan-format.md. No code is written before a developer approves the plan; the approval is recorded in the planned entry of each requirement's state file. The main agent then has each part written by its own sub-agent and checked against the test checklist and by a code reviewer that runs Claude Code's code-review skill and then the code checklist. VOGON has no code reviewer of its own. A developer's instruction that changes the plan sends it back for approval. All tests pass before the pull request is opened.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
vogon:init adds lines to the host conftest.py that copy each test's req and procedure marker ids into the JUnit XML properties (src/vogon/references/conftest.md). A test run records the commit it tested as the suite name, and vogon:release reports a suite name that is not the release commit. Where and how the suite runs is the project's choice; a pytest run that names the suite this way is:

pytest --junitxml=results.xml -o junit_suite_name=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

A run on a working tree with uncommitted changes is reported, because the commit then does not identify the code tested.

Where a test manager exists, VOGON uploads the JUnit XML unchanged and the test manager produces the traceability report (DEC-003). Where none exists, vogon trace joins the markers and results of one commit into the matrix, including every requirement with no test. It manages no test cases and records no approvals. The matrix is evidence, so it comes from this join or from the test manager, never from a model.

docs.title: Release
docs.text: vogon:release takes a release commit, a release name and the JUnit XML of a test run on that commit. Sub-agents draft each document documents.md lists from a read-only checkout of that commit, citing what each statement rests on, and evaluators check them. The skill produces the matrix, files documents, matrix and results, reads the filed copies back and tells each approver what waits. A plan whose requirements all have a released entry moves to vogon/plans/done/.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Contents .claude-plugin/ The marketplace listing. src/vogon/ The Claude Code plugin: skills, references, templates. src/docs/ Documentation source, markdown. src/html/ Marketing page source: index.html, img/. docs/ Build output. Rendered HTML, served by GitHub Pages. Never edit. vogon/ VOGON's own records: requirements, facts, constraints, decisions. tmp/ Working notes and plans. Gitignored, local only. assets/ Brand originals. Never published. .githooks/ The pre-commit hook that rebuilds docs/.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
uv sync
git config core.hooksPath .githooks

core.hooksPath points git at the hooks committed in .githooks/. It is a local setting, so it is set once per clone.

pyproject.toml exists for development only: it holds the dev dependency group.

docs.title: Building the site
docs.text:
make site     # src/docs/ -> docs/, then src/html/ copied over the top
make serve    # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000
make clean    # rm -rf docs/

docs/ is committed because Pages serves it from git. .githooks/pre-commit rebuilds and stages it when a commit touches src/docs/, src/html/ or mkdocs.yml. A failed build aborts the commit, and --strict makes a broken link fail it. A hand edit inside docs/ is overwritten by the next build.

mkdocs and mkdocs-material are in the dev dependency group, run through uv run --group dev, and uv.lock fixes their versions. uvx mkdocs resolves a fresh version each time, and the rendered output is committed, so it is not used.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
GitHub Pages, deploy from a branch: Settings → Pages → Source "Deploy from a branch", branch main, folder /docs.

src/html/index.html            → /
src/html/img/emblem.webp       → /img/emblem.webp
src/docs/user/install.md       → /user/install.html
src/docs/dev/architecture.md   → /dev/architecture.html
assets/                        → not served

src/html/.nojekyll copies through to docs/.nojekyll and stops GitHub re-running Jekyll over HTML that mkdocs already rendered. mkdocs-material writes its theme CSS and JS into docs/assets/, which is unrelated to the top-level assets/.

docs.title: The plugin
docs.text:
The repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. .claude-plugin/marketplace.json lists the plugin vogon, with source ./src/vogon:

src/vogon/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   name, version, description
├── references/                  rules shared by the skills
├── templates/                   templates of the host project's process files
└── skills/
    ├── init/                    SKILL.md
    ├── requirements/            SKILL.md, references/
    ├── approve/                 SKILL.md
    ├── next/                    SKILL.md
    ├── tests/                   SKILL.md, references/
    ├── implement/               SKILL.md, references/
    └── release/                 SKILL.md

Architecture describes the skills.

The version is in plugin.json and nowhere else. There is no wheel and no PyPI release.

Each release is tagged v<version>, with the version read from plugin.json, on the commit that sets it: v0.1.0 for version 0.1.0.

claude plugin validate .           # the marketplace listing
claude plugin validate src/vogon   # the plugin manifest

To test the plugin as a host project sees it, open Claude Code in a scratch git repository and run:

/plugin marketplace add /path/to/repo --scope project
/plugin install vogon@vogon --scope project

Claude Code copies the plugin into its cache at install, keyed by version. A change in the working tree reaches the scratch repository only after the plugin is uninstalled and installed again; /plugin update does nothing while the version is unchanged.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: Vocabulary defines the four kinds of record.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Records live in vogon/, in the host project's repository and in the VOGON project's alike.

Path Holds vogon/project/ vogon.yaml, the configuration, and the process files derived from the validation plan. See Architecture. checklists/ holds the project's own versions of the default checklists vogon/requirements/<module>/ Requirement records, one directory per module: each REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>.md with its state file REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>.json beside it, and test procedures kept in the repository vogon/facts/ Every FACT- vogon/constraints/ Every CON- vogon/decisions/ Every DEC- vogon/sources/ Held copies of the documents records cite: the validation plan, checked summaries of meetings, mail and chat, and attached files with their markdown copies. See Sources vogon/plans/ Plans for code, approved by the developers before the code is written; done/ holds the spent ones vogon/documents/<release>/ Drafted documents for one release, where the project has no document system vogon/logs/ Loop logs. Gitignored unless the project commits them vogon/tmp/ Working files deleted before the skill finishes: downloaded transcripts, mail and chat, draft test procedures, draft release documents and the release checkout. Gitignored

A record's identity is its id, not its path. Requirements are grouped by module; facts, constraints and decisions are flat, because one is often cited by several modules.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The rules a writing sub-agent and an evaluator apply to every record are in src/vogon/references/records.md: how a sentence is classified, the id and file name, each frontmatter field, the body blocks of each type and the suggested lengths. Every record also follows the writing standard, src/vogon/references/writing.md.

A sentence often states two kinds of record. "The test manager reports coverage from the link between a test issue and a requirement issue, so maintain that link from the test source" is a fact and a requirement, written as two records; the requirement names the fact in depends_on.

YAML frontmatter is read by the skills and scripts, and the markdown body by people. No field and no body line states that a record was approved or signed: approvals are in the state file.

source names every held document that states the record, not only the one it was drafted from, strongest authority first (Sources). A path in source asserts that the document says this, so only a passage that was read is cited.

references names the documents that say how the record is realised, such as the schema a decision settles. source names what the record came from; references names what elaborates it.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: status records whether the project is committed to the statement: active, withdrawn or {superseded_by: <id>}. A record is never deleted. Build progress is in the state file and the passing tests.

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text:
At vogon/requirements/<module>/REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>.md.

The requirement adds verification, the four risk fields (gxp_impact, gxp_impact_reason, risk, risk_reason), and the body blocks **Requirement.**, **Out of scope.** and **Acceptance criteria.**. **Out of scope.** names what the requirement does not cover, so that nobody builds or tests it. The risk method and levels come from requirements.md where the validation plan states them. Each expected value in the acceptance criteria is worked out from the requirement and its sources, never read off a run of the code, because a value taken from the code makes the test that asserts it unable to fail. The acceptance criteria are approved with the requirement.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
---
id: REQ-PRN-12
type: requirement
title: Print the sample id as a barcode on the tube label
modules: [PRN]
status: active
source:
  - vogon/sources/2026-09-15_sample_labelling.summary.md
verification: test
gxp_impact: data integrity
gxp_impact_reason: A wrong barcode attaches a result to the wrong sample.
risk: high
risk_reason: A mismatch harms the sample record, occurs whenever a label is
  reprinted from stale data, and is not visible to the person applying it.
---

# REQ-PRN-12: Print the sample id as a barcode on the tube label

**Requirement.** The label printer MUST encode the sample id stored for the
tube, and only that id, in a Code 128 barcode on its label.

**Out of scope.** The label layout, and printing labels for anything other
than sample tubes.

**Example.** Sample S-2026-00417 is registered. Its tube label carries a
barcode that a scanner reads as `S-2026-00417`.

**Acceptance criteria.**

- The barcode on a printed label decodes to the stored sample id.
- A label reprinted after the sample id was corrected decodes to the
  corrected id.
- A sample with no stored id produces no label and an error.

docs.title: State file
docs.text:
Each requirement has a state file beside its markdown file, named for the same id with .json. It records every step done to the requirement, in order. Entries are appended and never edited or removed. A withdrawal is the record's status, not a step. Every entry and its fields are defined in src/vogon/references/common.md, "State-file entries".

Where no tracker holds approvals, a requirement is approved when the state file on the default branch has an approved entry after its latest changed entry; an approved entry that only an open pull request holds does not count. Where a tracker holds approvals, the state file holds no approved entry and the tracker item is the record. For every entry, the pull request, commit or tracker item it names counts over the entry: a skill checks it before acting and reports any difference (src/vogon/references/common.md, "Start of every skill" and "Approval of a requirement").

docs.title: Domain fact, constraint and decision
docs.text: A fact is at vogon/facts/FACT-<NUMBER>.md, a constraint at vogon/constraints/CON-<NUMBER>.md, a decision at vogon/decisions/DEC-<NUMBER>.md, with no module in the id. A fact carries as_of, the date it was observed, so it can be checked again. A constraint carries imposed_by and lifts_when. A merged decision is never edited; a later decision supersedes it, and both files stay.

docs.title: Test procedure
docs.text: Where tests.md keeps test procedures in the repository, each is at vogon/requirements/<module>/TP-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>.md, beside the requirements it verifies, which its verifies field lists. Where they are kept in the tracker or test manager, the item key is the id and VOGON writes no file.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
An id is a type, an optional module, and a number:

<TYPE>-<NUMBER>
<TYPE>-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>

TYPE is REQ, FACT, CON, DEC, or TP for a test procedure. MODULE names the part of the system the record belongs to, in uppercase letters and digits; facts, constraints and decisions, and every record of a project without modules, omit it. The modules are listed in vogon.yaml, and a record may name only a listed module. NUMBER is compared numerically when ids are ordered. Numbers count separately per type and module.

vogon id <type> <module> gives the next number from every branch and the history. Two branches can take the same id before either pushes, so a skill runs vogon id --check and renumbers before it opens its pull request (src/vogon/references/common.md, "Commands").

Once merged, an id is permanent: never reused or renumbered, also after withdrawal. The file is named for the id alone, such as REQ-PRN-12.md, so that a changed title breaks no link. A record's history is its git history.

docs.title: Marketing page
docs.text: src/html/index.html is standalone: no build step, copied verbatim into docs/ by make site. It reads as an enterprise life-sciences SaaS page that is also a controlled document. It has a persistent document-control strip, SOP clause numbering (§1.0 …), square-cornered hairline panels, and two animations that run together when a change request is submitted: the REJECTED stamp lands (slam) and its card shakes (shk). Both are off under prefers-reduced-motion.

docs.title: Type and color
docs.text:
Archivo for display, Source Sans 3 for body, IBM Plex Mono for document metadata and CLI, Source Serif 4 italic for quotes.

Color tokens are sampled from the artwork: paper #FBFAF5, ink #101820, oxblood #971A1C, stamp #BF100F, slate #6E7B82, rule #DFDACF. Light and dark are both defined on :root. Fixed dark chrome (nav strip, footer, consent bar) uses the --dark-ground* tokens and stays dark in both themes.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Images are WebP in src/html/img/, referenced relatively as img/… so the paths survive the copy into docs/. Regenerate with ImageMagick from assets/images/ after adding artwork.

Most of the artwork was drawn on white paper, which glares on a dark page, so those figures have a dark twin, assets/images/<name>_dark.png, served as src/html/img/<name>_dark.webp where one exists. 03 and 08 are served dark as emblem_dark.webp and stamp-alpha_dark.webp. The twins were redrawn for dark ground; flood fills and lightness inversions were tried and rejected.

A dark twin must be the same pixel size as the light .webp beside it, because index.html carries one width/height pair for both sources:

magick identify -format '%wx%h' src/html/img/<name>.webp
magick assets/images/<name>_dark.png -resize '<W>x<H>!' \
  -quality 82 -define webp:method=6 src/html/img/<name>_dark.webp

Where the aspect ratios differ, as for 04, which is square in dark and 1200×1006 in light, centre-crop to the light ratio first (-gravity center -crop 1254x1051+0+0 +repage) rather than squashing.

emblem.webp (03) and stamp-alpha.webp (08) are transparent cutouts and both are white-keyed: the vogon's white shirt and the paper inside the stamp frame went with the background. That reads correctly on cream and leaves holes on dark ground. Their dark counterparts are made from the authored dark artwork: emblem_dark.webp is a circular mask of 03-vogon-icon_dark.png, and stamp-alpha_dark.webp takes its alpha from the brightest channel of 08-rejected-stamp_dark.png. The footer stamp uses the dark one unconditionally because the footer is --dark-ground in both themes. The rejection dialog keeps stamp-alpha.webp, which is the stronger red on its cream card.

A figure with a dark twin is served through <picture> with media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)", in index.html and in the README. There is no theme toggle, so the media query is the only mechanism that switches images. The CSS also has :root[data-theme="dark"] and :not([data-theme="light"]) rules, but nothing sets data-theme, so only the prefers-color-scheme branch takes effect.

docs.title: Lightbox
docs.text:
Every figure is click-to-enlarge. Wrap it in <div class="zoomfig" role="button" tabindex="0"> and the lightbox picks it up, captioned from the image's data-ref. The footer REJECTED stamp is one of these.

The lightbox fits a figure whole and never enlarges it past its own pixels, so a 1200px figure stops at 1200px on a wide monitor instead of being blurred by upscaling. Portrait figures are the exception: VGN-PROC-001 is a tall chart containing body text, and fitted to the dialog height it is unreadable. A figure taller than it is wide is sized to the dialog width instead, capped at 1.5× its own pixels, and the area scrolls. Clicking the figure does not close the dialog; only the backdrop does.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: A record cites the documents it came from, and those documents are held in the repository so the citation can be checked years later. The filing rules a writing sub-agent and an evaluator apply are in src/vogon/references/sources.md. What a citation means is in Records.

docs.title: Location and name
docs.text:
Every held document lives in vogon/sources/, flat. Its kind is in its frontmatter, not its directory, because a record cites a meeting summary and a standard the same way.

vogon/sources/2026-09-17_requirements_workshop.summary.md
vogon/sources/2026-04-02_electronic_records_procedure.pdf
vogon/sources/2026-04-02_electronic_records_procedure.md

The date is the document's own (meeting day, issue date), not the filing date, so the directory sorts chronologically and two versions differ by name.

docs.title: Original and markdown copy
docs.text:
A document that is not already markdown is held twice: the original as received, and a markdown copy beside it with the same stem. The original is the evidence. The markdown copy diffs and greps, and a reviewer sees in a pull request what a record was written from. Records cite the markdown copy.

A copy is never corrected by hand. A wrong copy is replaced by a better conversion, because a hand-edited copy no longer says what the original says and nothing shows it.

docs.title: Edits
docs.text: A held document is never changed, typos included. A corrected or reissued document is a new file with its own date. Records citing the old file keep citing it or are updated deliberately. A citation asserts that a specific document says something, and a document edited after the fact cannot support that.

docs.title: Meetings, mail and chat
docs.text:
A meeting, mail thread or chat channel is held only as a checked summary, and the download is deleted before the skill commits (src/vogon/references/sources.md, "Meetings, mail and chat"). A transcript holds personal remarks and discussion unrelated to the project, some countries restrict keeping it, and the meeting system keeps it under its own retention rule.

The summary is checked against the download before the download is deleted, because a statement the source did not make cannot be found afterwards. Records are drafted from the checked summary. A requirement drafted from a summary is binding once the Product Owner approves it; the meeting is only where it came from.

docs.title: Attached and shared files
docs.text: A file attached to a mail, posted in a chat, shared in a meeting or named by the developer is filed as its original and markdown copy, and kept. Its date is the file's own date.

docs.title: authority
docs.text: authority is regulation, standard, procedure, project or informal, strongest first. It decides what a record may claim from the document, and a source list is ordered by it. The table of what each value may support is in src/vogon/references/sources.md. An informal document is never the only support for a domain fact.

docs.title: Not held
docs.text: Documentation the project wrote about itself is not held: it lives in the project's documentation, and a record points at it with references. A document that cannot be redistributed, such as a licensed standard, is cited by identifier and clause.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text:
How to write a record is in Records.

Projects often keep four kinds of statement in one requirements list under one numbering. Most of those rows cannot be tested. VOGON keeps them as four kinds of record.

docs.title: The two projects
docs.text:
VOGON is one codebase installed into another, and both keep records in vogon/ in the same format, so the two are named apart.

VOGON project: this repository. VOGON's own code, documentation and records.

Host project: a project VOGON is installed into, holding that project's own code, tests and records. User project means the same thing; host project is the term used in the documentation.

A statement about vogon/ applies to both unless it names one.

docs.title: The four kinds of record
docs.text:
Everything written down that the system will be built from is one of four things. Each has its own id namespace and its own file. A test procedure is also a record, of type TP, defined under Tests below.

Requirement: something the system must do. Written as a MUST statement saying what has to be true and not how, so that a test could fail it. Ids are REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>, or REQ-<NUMBER> in a project without modules.

Domain fact: something true whether or not this project exists. "A test issue in the test manager is linked to the requirement issue it verifies" is a fact; nobody on the project chose it and no test of ours can fail it. Prefix FACT-.

Constraint: a limit imposed from outside that design cannot trade away: a regulation, a company procedure, or a platform behaviour. "Approval cannot be performed by a machine account" is a constraint. Prefix CON-.

Decision: a choice made among options, recorded with what the options cost and what the choice commits us to. Choosing not to build something is a decision. Prefix DEC-.

The checked summary or held document a record came from is a source (Sources). Records cite it; it is never a record itself.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
RFC 2119 as clarified by RFC 8174: only the uppercase form is binding, so an ordinary "must" or "should" in prose carries no weight.

Word Means MUST, MUST NOT A requirement. Binding. The only form a requirement record is written in SHOULD, SHOULD NOT A recommendation. Not binding, and not a requirement MAY Permission (no modal verb) A statement of fact, about the world or about something outside our control

"Results imported into the test manager sometimes arrive without a build identifier" has no modal verb, so it is a domain fact. "VOGON MUST reject a result import with no build identifier" is the requirement beside it.

VOGON writes MUST, not "shall". ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 uses "shall"; GAMP 5, EU Annex 11 and 21 CFR Part 11 prescribe no modal verb, only that a requirement be unambiguous, testable, uniquely identified and traceable.

docs.title: Compliance terms
docs.text: Term What it is GxP The umbrella label for regulations covering work a regulator relies on ICH The body that writes the guidelines the FDA, EMA and others adopt ISPE A pharmaceutical engineering industry association GAMP 5 ISPE's guide to validating a computerised system so an inspector accepts it. Second Edition, 2022. A guide, not a law GAMP category 5 Custom-written software, the category with the most scrutiny 21 CFR Part 11 The US regulation on electronic records and electronic signatures EU Annex 11 The European counterpart to Part 11 ALCOA+ A checklist of properties regulated data must have: attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, plus complete, consistent, enduring, available Validation Producing evidence that you specified what the system should do, built to that, and verified it CSV / CSA The two names for validating software in this industry; CSA is the FDA's more recent risk-based framing URS User Requirements Specification: the controlled document holding approved requirements RTM Requirements Traceability Matrix: requirement to design to test to result, for every requirement Tracker The issue tracker holding work items such as requirements, their priority and assignee, and where the project uses it for approval, their approval. For example Jira or GitHub Issues Test manager The system holding test cases, test runs and results, which produces the coverage and traceability reports. For example Xray. A project may have none Repository host The service holding the git repository and reviewing changes before they merge. For example GitHub Document system The controlled document management system where the validation package is filed and signed

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Term What it is Acceptance criteria The part of a requirement that states what must be tested. Approved with the requirement Test A pytest function. Its req marker names the requirements it verifies. A test with a req marker is the test case for those requirements Test procedure A document, not code: numbered steps in prose, each with its expected result, with an id and linked to its requirement. Projects call it a test script, test protocol or manual test case; VOGON says test procedure, because "script" reads as code. Written and approved as tests.md states

docs.title: Who signs what
docs.text:
A validated system's documents are signed by roles named in the validation plan. The skills use the Product Owner role, product_owner in vogon.yaml, for the approval of requirements. Every other approval comes from the plan, as the project process files state it. vogon.yaml lists the people who hold each role, so records and generated documents name the role and never the person. The roles below are common ones; a project uses the roles its plan names.

Role What this person normally does Formal role in validation System Owner One named person on the IT side. Answers for the software for as long as it runs: available, supported, secure, and changed only through change control Signs the technical documents and chairs the change control board. Cannot be empty at release Business Process Owner One named person from the business side who knows how the work is done and answers for that process Decides the finished system is fit to use. Cannot be empty at release IT Quality Manager One named person outside the build team. Checks that the validation process was followed: documents exist, were approved before use, and agree with each other Signs the validation plan and the summary report. Must be independent of the people building the system Business Quality Manager One named person outside the build team, on the business side. Checks that the process the system supports still complies Signs alongside the IT Quality Manager, under the same independence rule Change control board A standing group that meets after release. For each proposed change it decides whether the change is allowed and what has to be re-tested before it ships The mechanism by which a validated system is allowed to change. Required once the system is live Validation lead One named person who writes the validation plan and the summary report and assembles the evidence into a package someone can audit Author, not approver Subject Matter Expert Anyone who knows the domain or the technology well enough to write or review a document. Not an appointment Writes and reviews documents. Never approves them, because an approver may not be the author Product Owner One named person who owns the backlog and decides what gets built next Approves the requirements, with vogon:approve or in the tracker. vogon.yaml lists the holders under product_owner Test Lead One of the engineers, named to review the test procedures Approves the test procedures and test documents the validation plan assigns to this role, as tests.md and documents.md state. Never approves test procedures they wrote Code reviewer Any engineer other than the author of a change Approves the change on the repository host before it merges

The approver of a document answers for it and may not be its author. One person may hold several roles, provided Quality is independent of the people building the system and nobody approves their own work.

An electronic signature is not a typed name or a pasted image. The signer re-enters their own credentials, and what is stored against that version of that record is their printed name, the date and time, and what the signature means: authored, reviewed or approved. It cannot be moved onto a later edit.

docs.title: Where these terms come from
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, the requirements engineering standard: requirement attributes (identifier, statement, rationale, source, verification method, status), the characteristics a well-formed requirement has, and constraint as a defined term. Its "shall" convention is not followed here.
  • RFC 2119 and RFC 8174: MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and the rule that only the uppercase forms are binding.
  • ISPE GAMP 5, Second Edition (2022): user requirement, the requirements traceability matrix, and per-requirement risk classification.
  • The architecture decision record is a convention from a 2011 post by Michael Nygard, not a standard.
  • One file per record, named by id, grouped by id prefix follows Doorstop, the closest existing tool for keeping requirements in git.
  • domain fact is local to this project. The nearest standard equivalents are 29148's assumptions and dependencies and the business-analysis term domain knowledge, and neither names what these files hold.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
Documentation for people operating VOGON: installing it, running it, and producing the evidence your quality unit will ask for.

  • Installation

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: VOGON is a Claude Code plugin. It is installed into Claude Code, and it creates its records and configuration in the host project when it is set up. Nothing from the plugin is copied into the host project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Claude Code.
  • Git, for the repository the records live in.
  • uv, which runs VOGON's scripts.
  • Python 3.11 or later, which uv installs if it is missing.
  • An MCP server connected to Claude Code for each system role the project uses: tracker (for example Jira or GitHub Issues), test manager (for example Xray), document system, repository host (for example GitHub), meetings (for example Teams or Google Meet), mail (for example Outlook or Gmail) and chat (for example Teams or Slack). A role with no server is not used.
  • In the tracker and the test manager, every transition that records an approval asks the approver for their own credentials.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in the host project's repository and run:

/plugin marketplace add pcingola/vogon --scope project
/plugin install vogon@vogon --scope project

Both commands take --scope project. Without it they default to user scope, which enables VOGON in every project the user opens. With it they write the marketplace and the plugin into the host project's .claude/settings.json, and nothing into the user's settings:

{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "vogon": {"source": {"source": "github", "repo": "pcingola/vogon"}}
  },
  "enabledPlugins": {"vogon@vogon": true}
}

Commit that file. Claude Code then offers to install the plugin to every developer who opens the project, and VOGON is active in no other project. Claude Code keeps the downloaded plugin files in a cache under ~/.claude/plugins/; the cache does not enable the plugin anywhere.

docs.title: Set up a host project
docs.text: Ask Claude Code to set up VOGON. It runs the vogon:init skill. Architecture describes what setup does.
